intergrate this feedback into [@roadmap](file:///home/ethan/rustix/docs/roadmap/) : Architectural Areas to Watch (Milestones 3–6)The Preemption Gap Before Ring 3: Milestone 3 notes that timer preemption and IRQ-safe locking are deferred, while Milestone 4 introduces isolated user processes. Be careful here: until you finish those two unchecked items in M3, a single Ring 3 process running an infinite loop (loop {}) will lock up the entire machine because the timer interrupt cannot preempt it. Tackling IRQ-safe spinlocks (saving/restoring RFLAGS.IF) and preemptive PIT scheduling before running untrusted Ring 3 code will make your M4 process isolation genuinely protective.   Page-Table & Kernel-Mapping Cost at Scale: In Milestone 2, you cloned Limine's reachable page-table hierarchy into allocator-owned frames. When you implement per-process address spaces in Milestone 4, decide early how the upper-half kernel mappings are shared across every process CR3 (typically by sharing the top-level PML4 entries for the kernel half) so creating a process doesn't require deep-cloning the entire kernel page table tree on every spawn/fork.   Stack & Syscall Entry Edge Cases (SWAPGS): When setting up SYSCALL/SYSRET in Milestone 4, pay extra attention to SYSRET canonical-address validation on x86_64. If a user program manipulates RCX (the return RIP) to a non-canonical address before invoking SYSCALL, Intel CPUs will raise a #GP while still in Ring 0 using the user's RSP unless you validate RCX canonicality in software before executing SYSRET or use IRETQ for non-standard returns.   Static Binaries & Storage Footprint: Using statically linked ELF64 binaries (.bin and .app) with embedded resources avoids building a dynamic linker (ld.so) early on. Just keep in mind that once you build your on-disk filesystem in Milestone 5, statically linking librustix and formatting/UI code into dozens of separate utility binaries (cp, mv, mkdir, etc.) will make your disk image grow quickly—keep librustix lean and #[no_std]-friendly.   M5 Scope Creep: Milestone 5 packs in VFS, PCI discovery, DMA ownership, virtio-blk, an on-disk filesystem, permissions/sticky bits, a CSPRNG, wall-clock time, and ACPI FADT shutdown/reboot. Consider splitting M5 into two clean checkpoints—M5a (PCI/DMA + Block Driver + Read-Only/Basic VFS) and M5b (Writable Filesystem + Permissions + CSPRNG/RTC/ACPI Power)—so your vertical slices stay small and verifiable.

    73	## Engineering rules
    74	
    75	### Keep changes incremental and coherent
    76	
    77	1. Inspect the relevant source, tests, docs, and call sites before editing.
    78	2. State assumptions, invariants, and failure behavior for new kernel interfaces.
    79	3. Prefer small vertical slices that compile and can be tested over broad scaffolding or placeholder APIs.
    80	4. Update tests and documentation alongside behavior changes.
    81	5. Do not change unrelated code, rename files gratuitously, add speculative features, or rewrite project history.
    82	6. Do not commit or create branches unless the user explicitly asks.
    83	
    84	### Rust and dependency policy
    85	
    86	- Preserve the kernel's `no_std`/freestanding constraints. Do not introduce `std` into kernel code.
    87	- Prefer `core` and existing in-tree abstractions. Do not add third-party Rust dependencies without a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
    88	- Keep the Crabshell parser independent of kernel I/O and VFS implementation. Kernel execution belongs in `src/shell.rs` or an appropriate kernel service.
    89	- Do not add allocation-dependent APIs before a real heap exists. Fixed-capacity structures must document their limits and exhaustion behavior.
    90	- Respect the workspace structure and the host-testable `rustix-kernel` library versus freestanding `rustix` binary boundary.
    91	
    92	### Unsafe and hardware code
    93	
    94	Unsafe code is expected only at explicit hardware, boot-protocol, assembly, or raw-memory boundaries. Keep each unsafe block narrow and document the invariant that makes it sound. Do not add broad `unsafe impl`, mutable global references, unchecked pointer arithmetic, or unreviewed inline/global assembly.

    96	Before changing boot or memory code, account for these facts:
    97	
    98	- Limine fills response pointers before `_start`; the request records must remain writable in the ELF image.
    99	- Rustix validates nullness, alignment, counts, arithmetic, and physical ranges, but cannot prove that a non-null bootloader pointer is readable.
   100	- Physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)` and must use checked arithmetic.
   101	- Only regions classified `Usable` may enter the frame allocator. ACPI, bootloader-reclaimable, framebuffer, reserved, unknown, and other types are not free frames.
   102	- A `Frame` is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. HHDM access is allowed only through checked full-frame token-based paths that rely on the documented Limine contract; never access arbitrary physical addresses. Do not change CR3 until a complete, reviewed transition mapping policy and ownership proof exist.
   103	- The kernel currently inherits Limine's page tables. Do not casually replace or mutate them: preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response data, exception stacks, and mappings needed to continue execution.
   104	- Exceptions remain fatal-only. The single-vCPU APIC path enables only configured, registered routes after IRQ dispatch/EOI setup and tests. Do not broaden IRQ use or add preemption without a reviewed ownership, synchronization, and validation plan.
   105	- The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.
   106	
   107	For hardware changes, document assumptions about CPU mode, selectors, stacks, page permissions, interrupt state, and failure handling. Avoid new architecture mechanisms that cannot be statically reviewed or validated.
   108

   110	
   111	- Crabshell is presently a kernel-mode serial shell, not a userspace program or a POSIX shell.
   112	- Its parser is a separate `no_std`, allocation-free crate; retain that boundary.
   113	- The RAM filesystem is volatile and bounded. Preserve explicit errors and test capacity, path, and mutation edge cases.
   114	- Do not imply persistence, permissions, links, process launching, or shell features that do not exist.
   115	- Update the parser tests and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` when adding or changing commands.
   116

   118	
   119	Run the narrowest relevant checks first, then broaden them. From the repository root, the supported commands are:
   120	
   121	```sh
   122	just fmt
   123	just test
   124	just check

    10	depends on it. Step 2 holds for small edits, follow-up work, and tasks that already

    18	    entire graph neighbors --repo . --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --symbol <Name> --direction in

pub const fn is_canonical_virtual_address(address: u64, address_bits: u8) -> bool {
    if address_bits == 0 || address_bits > 64 {
        return false;
    }
    if address_bits == 64 {
        return true;
    }

    let sign_bit = (address >> (address_bits - 1)) & 1;
    let upper_bits = address >> address_bits;
    let expected_upper_bits = if sign_bit == 0 {
        0
    } else {
        u64::MAX >> address_bits
    };
    upper_bits == expected_upper_bits
}

   168	## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI
   169	
   170	Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions.

   184	- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, user/kernel fault separation, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

   187	
   188	A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

     1	# x86_64 drivers
     2	
     3	## Driver boundary
     4	
     5	Rustix keeps privileged platform access in `src/arch/x86_64/`. Device-facing routines should be small, explicit about polling/interrupt assumptions, and separated from policy such as terminal input or process I/O. The current drivers are intentionally early-boot building blocks, not a finished device model.
     6	
     7	## Implemented drivers
     8	
     9	| Driver | Source | Status and limits |
    10	|---|---|---|
    11	| 16550-compatible COM1 serial | [`src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs`](../../src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs) | Polling formatted output and early-boot input; after APIC setup, IRQ4 drains RX bytes into a bounded queue and wakes the cooperative shell. Bounded transmit waits remain in use. |
    12	| x86 port I/O primitives | [`src/arch/x86_64/io.rs`](../../src/arch/x86_64/io.rs) | Small unsafe `in`/`out` wrappers used by platform drivers. |
    13	| PS/2-compatible keyboard controller | [`src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs`](../../src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs) | Bounded IRQ1 drain into a raw-scancode queue, plus non-blocking polling fallback; filters auxiliary-device and controller-error bytes. |
    14	| Local APIC, I/O APIC, and PIT | [`src/arch/x86_64/apic.rs`](../../src/arch/x86_64/apic.rs) | One-vCPU MADT-routed IRQ delivery; PIC routes remain masked. PIT supplies the approximately 100 Hz scheduler tick. |
    15	
    16	The PS/2 driver assumes a legacy controller is present. Initialization uses bounded waits; raw scancodes are not translated, and USB HID is unsupported. UART and keyboard IRQ paths use bounded queues and notify the cooperative scheduler; polling remains available for early boot/fallback.
    17	
    18	## Driver development rules
    19	
    20	- Keep port I/O, MMIO, DMA, and interrupt entry points in architecture/device modules; do not expose raw I/O ports to generic kernel services.
    21	- Document required privilege level, device assumptions, concurrency/interrupt context, and whether a call can block.
    22	- Bound waits in early boot, avoid allocation in low-level paths, and propagate/report device absence rather than hanging startup.
    23	- Separate raw hardware events from key mapping, terminal semantics, and user-visible input policy.
    24	- Add emulator/hardware tests when an integration harness exists; host tests alone cannot validate port I/O.
    25	
    26	## Planned driver work
    27	
    28	`src/time.rs` provides host-tested PIT divisor selection and monotonic tick arithmetic; the x86_64 APIC driver programs the PIT and delivers live ticks. This is a monotonic tick source, not wall-clock time. Timer preemption and SMP require separately designed locking and per-CPU rules. Framebuffer/console output, PCI discovery, storage, and networking remain future drivers; no support for those devices is implied.

````rustix/docs/architecture/overview.md
     1	# Architecture overview
     2	
     3	## Goals
     4	
     5	Rustix is a from-scratch operating system project with its own kernel, written in Rust. The intended initial platform is 64-bit x86 (`x86_64`), with a Unix-like process and file-descriptor model. The kernel should eventually own machine initialization, physical and virtual memory management, interrupt handling, scheduling, system calls, and device policy. A bootloader is a transport into the kernel, not a replacement for those facilities.
     6	
     7	Unix-like is a compatibility direction. It does **not** mean the current kernel is POSIX-compliant, nor does it commit the project to a particular existing kernel's internals. Compatibility profiles and a userland should be defined only after the underlying process, descriptor, and syscall semantics are implemented and tested.
     8	
     9	## Current implementation
    10	
    11	1. Cargo builds a `no_std`, `no_main` ELF for `x86_64-unknown-none` and uses Limine for the boot handoff.
    12	2. `_start` initializes COM1 and exception diagnostics, captures a validated boot snapshot and frame-allocator state, activates a clone of Limine's page tables, configures the validated single-vCPU APIC/PIT path, installs bounded heap growth, and starts the shell runtime when timer and UART IRQ setup succeed.
    13	3. Crabshell reads an ASCII command line from COM1's bounded IRQ queue and blocks cooperatively while idle; polling remains fallback. It supports basic navigation, directory creation/listing, and text-file operations.
    14	4. The separately packaged `crabshell` `no_std` crate parses commands without allocation or dependence on kernel I/O, making that layer reusable by a future graphical frontend.
    15	5. The kernel library contains checked memory accounting, bounded ACPI/IRQ/time/input/scheduler policies, heap tests, and the bounded VFS implementation, covered by host-side tests.
    16	
    17	The shell and filesystem run in kernel mode. Files exist only in RAM and disappear at reboot. Bootstrap exceptions remain fatal-only; selected timer/UART/PS/2 IRQ routes are enabled after APIC, IDT, and handler setup. The single-vCPU scheduler is cooperative, not preemptive. The active page tables are an owned clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy, with bounded active mapping and a global heap consisting of a 256 KiB BSS arena plus up to 1 MiB of frame-backed growth. There is no clean-room address-space policy, general-purpose MMIO/mapping policy, frame reclamation, timer preemption, SMP, user/kernel isolation, syscall ABI, on-disk filesystem, network stack, or userspace process.
    18	
    19	## Intended layers (planned)
    20	
    21	```text
    22	User programs and system utilities
    23	        | versioned syscall ABI
    24	Kernel services: processes, descriptors, VFS, IPC, signals
    25	        | explicit ownership and authorization checks
    26	Core kernel: scheduler, virtual memory, physical frames, interrupts
    27	        | narrow architecture abstractions
    28	x86_64 platform: paging, exceptions, timers, AP startup, drivers
    29	        | Limine boot handoff only
    30	Firmware and hardware
    31	```
    32	
    33	The diagram is a target decomposition, not a claim that those layers are implemented. Architecture-independent policy should live in safe Rust where possible; privileged instructions and raw device access should stay in small, reviewed architecture modules.
    34	
    35	## Design constraints
    36	
    37	- **Freestanding:** kernel code does not link `std`; global allocation is bounded, frame-backed growth is explicit, and allocation is forbidden in IRQ/exception context.
    38	- **Explicit unsafe boundaries:** raw pointers from boot protocol responses and x86 port I/O are unsafe. Each use must document its preconditions and remain short-lived.
    39	- **Fail visibly:** early boot failures should produce serial diagnostics where possible and then halt, rather than continue with invalid machine state.
    40	- **Checked arithmetic:** physical ranges, sizes, and address translations must reject overflow.
    41	- **No premature ABI:** userspace interfaces stay unstable until process lifetime, error conventions, copy-in/copy-out, and versioning are designed together.
    42	- **Hardware-independent tests:** parsing, range arithmetic, and policy should be testable as ordinary host-side Rust wherever possible.
    43	
    44	## Boot and CPU assumptions
    45	
    46	The current target is x86_64, with a 4 KiB page-oriented linker layout and no red zone. Limine performs the initial platform setup required by its protocol. Rustix must not assume that receiving a memory-map response means it owns the loader's page tables or can overwrite reserved regions. The bootstrap enables only validated single-vCPU APIC routes after their handlers and EOI paths are ready; it does not start application processors or enable timer preemption.
    47	
    48	See [Boot protocol](boot.md), [Memory management](memory.md), [x86_64 drivers](drivers.md), [Crabshell](crabshell.md), and [the roadmap](../roadmap/README.md) for subsystem boundaries and planned acceptance criteria.

````

```rustix/docs/architecture/memory.md
    23	## Active-root preservation and remaining limits
    24	
    25	The transition clones the complete reachable inherited hierarchy rather than building a clean address space. It preserves all reachable present leaves and non-present entries, owns each cloned intermediate table, and fails closed on malformed entries, unsupported page sizes, cross-level table aliases, or fixed-capacity exhaustion. Kernel text/rodata/data HHDM aliases are then adjusted to avoid writable-executable aliases. Limine's original root and leaf frames remain intact.
    26	
    27	- **Kernel ELF image:** `linker.ld` places `.text`, `.rodata`, `.limine_requests`, `.data`, `.bss`, and `.got` in three `PT_LOAD` segments: RX text, read-only rodata, and RW data/BSS. It exports `__kernel_start` and `__kernel_end` around the complete loadable image, plus page-aligned bounds for each segment. `BootInfo` checks that Limine's reported virtual base matches the linker start, validates ordered contiguous segment bounds covering the rounded image, derives corresponding half-open physical ranges from the executable physical base with checked arithmetic, and validates canonical virtual and reported physical address widths. The release ELF and QEMU runtime report both showed the three aligned ranges on 2026-10-21. The RX, R/NX, and RW/NX labels describe the linker segment intent; these are linker/boot metadata, not proof that the inherited page tables map every page or enforce those permissions, nor proof that loader pointers are readable. The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.
    28	- **Active stack and `BootInfo`:** The assembly `_start` shim captures Limine's entry `RSP` before any Rust prologue. Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. Rustix requests a 256 KiB Limine stack and requires the stack-size response; `BootInfo` records and validates that requested span through the HHDM, including its `BootloaderReclaimable` backing. The loader may allocate more, and no guard page is inferred. QEMU transition tests walk all 64 requested stack pages.
    29	- **Kernel static data:** `RAM_FILESYSTEM`, GDT, IDT, TSS, the ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static BSS/data in the kernel image. Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.
    30	- **Limine request data:** request records are in the kernel's writable `.limine_requests` segment. Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.
    31	- **Inherited page tables:** Limine places its page tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but their layout is unspecified. `BootInfo` captures raw CR3 and validates the decoded root address and active low-bit mode. The default boot path clones all reachable page-table pages into allocator-owned frames and preserves all leaf entries, then changes only the kernel-image HHDM alias permission bits while retaining cache attributes. It verifies kernel segments, the requested stack span, and the candidate-root HHDM alias before switching; afterward it verifies CR3 and the critical paths again. The inherited root and its backing pages remain untouched and are not reclaimed.
    32	- **Devices:** COM1 uses x86 port I/O and needs no MMIO virtual mapping. Rustix does not currently request or use a framebuffer. Any future framebuffer or device-register mapping needs an explicit physical range and cache policy.
    33	
    34	## Permissions and cache policy of the active clone
    35	
    36	The active root preserves Limine's inherited kernel virtual mappings and their cache attributes. Before switching, Rustix requires NXE and enforces the linker permissions for every kernel-image HHDM alias: text and rodata are read-only/NX, and data/BSS/GOT are RW/NX. This prevents writable-executable aliases without discarding the HHDM alias. Huge-page leaves are split as necessary; unaffected entries retain their mappings and PAT/MTRR effective types. The remainder of the HHDM and all non-kernel aliases remain as Limine supplied them, so this is not yet a comprehensive Rustix mapping policy.
    37	
    38	Preserve the inherited PAT/MTRR configuration during the first transition. The boot report validates captured registers and computes a diagnostic effective type from the active PAT/MTRR values under normal caching. A separate pure selector can choose an index whose effective type remains uniform across an aligned physical range; the selector itself does not inspect PTEs or aliases. The opt-in `just frame-smoke` probe now compares effective types of the inherited kernel and HHDM aliases for kernel-image pages, but it is not a full alias inventory. The pure combination follows Intel SDM Table 11-7; it is not a generic rule for legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations. The active transition retains the inherited PAT and MTRR state and changes no cache-selection bits. The page-table split copies large-page PAT selection to the equivalent 4 KiB/2 MiB entries. Future MMIO mappings must still use explicit device ranges and a verified cache policy; do not infer MMIO from generic reserved memory-map entries. COM1 uses port I/O and requires no MMIO mapping.
    39	
    40	Do not use huge pages in the first root; add them only when physical coverage, permissions, and cache attributes are uniform across the entire huge-page extent. Future Rustix-owned downward-growing stacks should have at least one 4 KiB unmapped guard page below them. The Limine bootstrap stack has no known guard, so none may be assumed there.
    41	
    42	Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. `src/paging.rs` builds an owned clone in allocator-issued frames, can split inherited large pages to update leaf permissions, and supports transactional 4 KiB map/unmap operations before activation. The default boot path validates critical translations and kernel alias permissions, switches CR3 while invalidating stale global translations via a CR4.PGE toggle when needed, verifies the active root, and retains its frame tokens for the active lifetime. The inherited root and backing memory remain intact. This preserves inherited mappings rather than constructing a new address space; broader mapping inventory, non-kernel permission policy, reclamation, and a general mapping service remain future work.
    43	
    44	## Planned memory layers
    45	
    46	1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.
    47	2. **Frame allocator integration:** the bounded core is initialized from `BootInfo`; table and leaf mappings use allocator-issued tokens. The active mapping smoke validates one owned page's map/access/unmap/reclamation path.
    48	3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix runs on an active clone of Limine's hierarchy and hardens kernel-image HHDM aliases. Narrow active owned-page map/unmap operations invalidate the local TLB; this is not a clean-room address-space policy or general MMIO subsystem.
    49	4. **Heap:** a 256 KiB BSS arena with 128 allocation records is backed by a bounded, demand-mapped extension of up to 1 MiB. Host tests and QEMU cover growth, reuse, exhaustion, and failed growth. The global allocator is not IRQ-safe and must not be called in interrupt context.
    50	5. **Process address spaces:** isolate userspace; define copy-in/copy-out helpers and never treat user pointers as kernel references.
    51	
    52	## Invariants to preserve
    53	
    54	- Physical ranges use checked arithmetic and the half-open convention `[start, end)`.
    55	- Only complete frames in validated `Usable` regions enter the allocator; the first MiB remains reserved. Firmware and loader-reclaimable regions are not silently promoted to free memory.
    56	- Under the single-allocator-per-physical-map contract, a frame is represented by one allocator-free range or one caller-owned, non-copyable `Frame` token. Only a successful `deallocate` transfers the token back to the allocator; errors return the token and leave allocator ranges and accounting unchanged. The current public constructor relies on callers to enforce unique allocator instances.
    57	- `allocate` returns `None` on frame exhaustion. Metadata-capacity exhaustion is an explicit error, never silent loss of a frame.
    58	- A `Frame` address is physical, not directly dereferenceable. HHDM translation and table access are limited to checked full-frame token-based paths that rely on Limine's documented mapping contract. Candidate mutations are allowed only before activation and only in owned tables. The active cloned root retains its ownership tokens and rejects mutation/release until an explicit, reviewed CR3 transition away from it.
    59	- Mapping changes validate alignment, canonical addresses, ownership, and permissions before touching tables.
    60	- User-controlled addresses are validated on every syscall boundary; prior validation is not a substitute for access checks during later copies.
    61	- Tests cover unaligned edges, exact-boundary allocations, arithmetic overflow, overlaps, exhaustion, and unchanged state/ownership on failure.
    62	
    63	The active root is a full clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy with kernel HHDM alias W^X hardening, not a clean-room Rustix address space. Heap growth is bounded to a fixed virtual reservation and 1 MiB of frame-backed pages. Broader alias/MMIO coverage, frame reclamation, and physical-hardware validation remain outstanding.

# Rustix roadmap

This roadmap describes an incremental path from the current bare-metal kernel to a useful Unix-like operating system. It is a dependency plan, not a schedule or a claim of compatibility. Features become current only after the implementation, tests, and exit criteria below agree.

## How to read status

- A checked box means the source/design work exists; it does **not** imply the code compiled, linked, booted, or passed an integration test.
- A milestone is not complete until its stated exit criteria are met and the evidence is recorded.
- Hardware work needs target build and emulator evidence. Host tests cannot validate privileged instructions, bootloader pointers, page tables, device I/O, or exception-entry assembly.
- Future work is intentionally not represented by placeholder APIs or dummy implementations.

## Current status

- **Milestone 0: local exit criteria met from a clean detached worktree; hosted CI observed.** On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 from both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory. On 2026-11-06, GitHub Actions run [#5](https://github.com/JustEthanCodes/rustix/actions/runs/42288095710) completed successfully on `dev` at `770f9c742dd07a00f6b53274ea05a1eca010d146`; its `kernel-and-boot-smoke` job ran `just verify`. This verifies hosted CI on that remote commit, not today’s uncommitted changes.
- **Milestone 1: validation criteria met for the current Limine path.** The bounded boot snapshot, memory-range classification, and CPUID reporting were covered by host tests and QEMU reporting; the Limine pointer-readability trust boundary remains explicit.
- **Milestone 2: local exit criteria met on 2026-10-24; hosted CI observed, physical-hardware validation pending.** The boot path owns and activates a clone of Limine's reachable page-table hierarchy, preserves inherited mappings, hardens kernel HHDM aliases to R/NX or RW/NX while retaining PAT attributes, invalidates stale translations on CR3 transitions, and retains table-frame tokens. `just verify`, `just frame-smoke`, and `just fault-smoke` passed after final review; QEMU exercised the active-PCID/CR3 invalidation path with CR4.PGE clear. The PGE-toggle path is statically reviewed but was not exercised by this QEMU configuration. The successful 2026-11-06 hosted `just verify` run covers the published Milestone 2 state, but not today's uncommitted changes. Broad mapping policy, reclamation, IRQ-safe allocation, and physical-hardware validation remain outside this milestone's completed scope.
- **Milestone 3: local exit criteria met on 2026-11-07; hosted CI and physical-hardware validation remain pending.** `just verify` passed with 127 host tests, the `x86_64-unknown-none` check, BIOS and OVMF boot smokes, active-map/TLB invalidation, cooperative thread/wait-queue tests, and UART/PS/2 input wakeup. OVMF validated MADT/APIC routing, PIT ticks and EOI, guarded cooperative stacks, frame-backed heap growth, and shell input without busy-polling. Timer preemption, IRQ-safe locking for future preemption, and SMP remain deferred. See the evidence and limits below. **Milestones 4 and later: planned.** There is no ARM64 platform support, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, GUI, or networking stack.

## Dependency path

```text
Reliable boot
    -> validated boot state
    -> owned mappings + frame allocation + heap + fault diagnostics
    -> timer/IRQ model + scheduler + IRQ-safe locking + timer preemption
    -> isolated processes + syscall ABI
    -> M5a PCI/DMA + block I/O + read-only/basic VFS
    -> M5b writable filesystem + permissions + platform services
    -> userland utilities
    -> graphical terminal and other optional services
```

Some device-driver work can proceed in parallel after the core ownership, locking, and testing rules exist. It must not bypass them with direct, unreviewed hardware access.

## Milestone 3 — IRQs, time, and kernel scheduling (local exit criteria met)

Do not enable interrupts as a side effect of installing exception gates. IRQ delivery needs its own controller, acknowledgement, masking, ownership, and synchronization design.

### Implementation and remaining work

The current source includes host-tested bounded ACPI parsing and span authorization, a boot-only read-only/NX ACPI reader that copies MADT data into owned state, xAPIC/I/O APIC routing, allocated IRQ dispatch and acknowledgement, a PIT timer, a cooperative scheduler, guarded thread stacks, bounded frame-backed heap growth, and interrupt-driven UART/PS/2 queues. On 2026-11-07, `just verify` passed on the final integrated tree, including active mapping/TLB, cooperative thread, and UART/PS/2 input QEMU smokes. The work-item boxes record source work and observed evidence; deferred timer preemption and SMP are not part of the completed single-vCPU cooperative slice.

**Ring 3 safety gate:** the completed cooperative slice is not sufficient to run general or untrusted user code. Do not start a Ring 3 process until both unchecked locking and timer-preemption work below are complete and validated. With cooperative-only scheduling, a user process that never yields can monopolize the CPU; enabling timer IRQ delivery without IRQ-safe synchronization would instead expose kernel state to interrupt-time deadlocks or races.

- [x] Use the existing single-vCPU QEMU `q35` configuration with the local APIC and MADT-described I/O APIC; keep legacy PIC routing masked. OVMF smokes observed timer and device IRQ delivery.
- [x] Read bounded ACPI tables through the validated read-only/NX path. The reader checks table bounds/signatures/checksums and copies the required MADT data into owned state; host tests cover malformed tables and span authorization, and OVMF reports the copied MADT.
- [x] Parse the selected machine's MADT topology and interrupt-source overrides. Host parser tests and OVMF boot cover the data used by APIC routing; FADT/HPET/MCFG work remains limited to this milestone's needs.
- [x] Add fixed-capacity IRQ vector ownership, masked-first controller routes, dispatch, spurious/unexpected-vector handling, and EOI. OVMF observed timer IRQ delivery and acknowledgement; input routes are also tested.
- [x] Route an approximately 100 Hz 8254 PIT through the I/O APIC and maintain atomic monotonic ticks. Host tests cover divisor and elapsed-time arithmetic, including fractional-tick rounding drift; OVMF verifies live timer delivery and EOI. Wall-clock time remains separate and is not provided.
- [x] Add bounded wait queues, cooperative sleep/wakeup, and event handoff; host scheduler tests and OVMF `thread-smoke` cover wakeup and timed sleep.
- [ ] Establish IRQ-safe lock primitives and broader context-specific locking rules before enabling timer preemption. Define interrupt-state save/restore semantics (including restoring the prior RFLAGS.IF state rather than unconditionally enabling interrupts), lock ordering, and which locks may be taken from IRQ context; the current heap is not IRQ-safe.
- [x] Implement owned-frame active map/unmap with explicit mapping/cache policy, transactional rollback, and local TLB invalidation. Host tests cover failure rollback; `active-map-smoke` passed live mapping, access, invalidation, and reclamation in QEMU.
- [x] Extend the 256 KiB bootstrap heap with a bounded 1 MiB frame-backed, demand-mapped region. Host tests cover growth, reuse, and failed growth; `thread-smoke` observed bootstrap exhaustion, growth, and reuse.
- [x] Keep allocator operations out of IRQ/exception handlers; handlers use bounded, allocation-free work, and the heap contract explicitly forbids IRQ-context allocation. Exhaustion is fallible at the allocator boundary. The heap is not IRQ-safe; timer preemption remains disabled.
- [x] Keep bootloader-reclaimable and ACPI memory, the active bootstrap stack, and Limine's inherited page-table root reserved; the active cloned root retains its owned table frames and does not reclaim the old root or inherited leaf frames.
- [x] Add single-vCPU cooperative threads with owned guarded stacks, lifecycle, yield, event wait/wakeup, timed sleep, and context-switch tests. The OVMF thread smoke passed these paths.
- [ ] Add timer-driven preemption only after locking, stack, timer, wait-queue, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests. Verify that a non-yielding task is preempted and that IRQ/exception paths cannot deadlock on locks held by interrupted code. This is a hard prerequisite for running general Ring 3 programs in Milestone 4. SMP remains a separate later sub-milestone.
- [x] Implement interrupt-driven UART RX and PS/2 raw-scancode queues with bounded buffers and scheduler event wakeups; preserve polling fallback. OVMF `input-smoke` sends a shell command over UART and verifies a PS/2 make scancode after the shell blocks for input.

**Exit criteria:** the single-vCPU QEMU `q35` configuration validates the selected APIC routing, PIT tick, and IRQ acknowledgement; host/QEMU tests cover ACPI bounds and malformed tables, mapping rollback/TLB behavior, heap exhaustion, wait-queue wakeups, and cooperative context switching. Interrupt-driven input is tested without busy-polling, and no heap allocation occurs in IRQ/exception context. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

---

## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI

Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions. Ring 3 execution is blocked on completing Milestone 3's IRQ-safe locking and timer-preemption items: a non-yielding user task must not be able to monopolize the machine, and preemption must not introduce interrupt-time lock deadlocks.

### Planned work

- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path. If using `SYSCALL`/`SYSRET`, specify `SWAPGS` entry/exit state transitions and how exceptions/NMIs during the transition are handled; validate user `RCX` (return RIP) and `RSP` canonicality and bounds before `SYSRET`, and use a safe `IRETQ` path or terminate/reject malformed returns when required.
- [ ] Define per-process address-space construction without deep-cloning the entire kernel page-table tree for every process. Choose a validated kernel-half sharing policy (for example, shared upper-level entries backed by immutable kernel subtrees), while keeping user mappings process-private; specify table ownership/lifetime, teardown, permission invariants, and TLB invalidation before sharing any page-table levels.
- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
- [ ] Load statically linked ELF64 executables with checked `PT_LOAD` bounds, alignment, permissions, and entry points; reject malformed binaries safely. Use `.bin` for command-line programs and `.app` for GUI applications as role-based filename suffixes for the same underlying format. `.app` is a Rustix single-file application suffix, not an Apple/macOS app bundle; initially require application resources to be embedded or absent.
- [ ] Add user-mode exception handling: faults attributable to Ring 3 terminate the offending process with a reported status, while faults in kernel mode remain fatal. Test page faults, general-protection faults, invalid opcodes, and divide errors from both privilege levels.
- [ ] Define user virtual-memory regions, stack bounds/guard behavior, and a minimal anonymous allocation interface such as `mmap`/`munmap` (or a documented equivalent) before running general user programs. Add bounds, permissions, exhaustion, and teardown tests.
- [ ] Add a small, `no_std`-friendly shared userspace runtime crate (for example, `librustix`) for process entry, syscall wrappers, panic handling, common I/O/formatting, and a user allocator backed by the anonymous mapping interface. Keep it separate from kernel internals and use it from independent application crates; initial executables remain statically linked ELF64 binaries, with application resources embedded or absent.
- [ ] Keep the first user-visible target as a minimal `init` executable loaded from a bounded boot payload or other reproducible non-filesystem source; persistent filesystem loading and ordinary command utilities follow in Milestones 5 and 6.
- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, user/kernel fault separation, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

### First user-visible target

A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.

---

## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership

Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.

### M5a — PCI/DMA, block I/O, and read-only/basic VFS

- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
- [ ] Establish bounded PCI/device discovery, including checked ACPI MCFG handling where required, before adding PCI-backed devices. Keep discovery separate from individual driver policy.
- [ ] Define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, device reset, and error handling before any device can DMA into kernel memory. Scope and test the trust assumptions; do not equate PCI enumeration with safe DMA.
- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk) on top of the shared PCI/DMA foundations.
- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format before implementing writable storage. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior; begin with a read-only mount and bounded metadata parsing.
- [ ] Test read-only mount, lookup, and read behavior against reproducible images, including malformed metadata and I/O errors. Do not expose write operations in this slice.
- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing filesystem operations to applications.

### M5b — writable filesystem, permissions, and platform services

- [ ] On detected corruption, report the failure and refuse writable mounting rather than attempting automatic repair. Plan a separate offline checker/repair tool; do not repair data implicitly.
- [ ] Define crash-safe atomic replacement or equivalent transactional behavior for critical files such as account metadata and credentials. Flush the new data before replacing the old file, and test interruption at each update stage.
- [ ] Define explicit no-space errors and partial-write behavior. Never silently discard or overwrite existing user data to recover space.
- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot and failure-injection integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.

- [ ] Define the planned top-level filesystem layout: `/home`, `/root`, `/etc`, `/usr`, `/dev`, `/proc`, `/sys`, `/tmp`, `/var`, `/run`, `/mnt`, `/media`, and `/boot`, plus `/usr/sbin`. Document that `/proc` and `/sys` are future virtual interfaces, `/dev` exposes device interfaces, `/tmp` and `/run` are volatile, and mount-point and boot-file usage depends on later storage/boot design.
- [ ] Specify filesystem ownership and permission metadata. Support owner/group/other read, write, and execute permissions, default creation modes/umask, and the directory sticky bit. Use sticky-directory semantics for `/tmp` (mode equivalent to `01777`) and later `/home/Public/`, so users can create entries without removing or renaming another user's files.
- [ ] Specify that `/etc` and `/usr` are root-owned and writable only by root, while normal users may read configuration and execute permitted programs. Keep readable account metadata separate from a root-only credential file containing password hashes. Reserve `/usr/Apps` for globally installed `.app` GUI applications and `/usr/bin` for globally installed `.bin` command-line tools; `/usr/sbin` is reserved for system-administration tools if needed.
- [ ] Provide a trustworthy CSPRNG before password hashing or security-sensitive random values. Evaluate validated entropy sources (for example, supported CPU randomness instructions or a virtio RNG device) as inputs; do not treat one hardware source alone as a complete CSPRNG. Test initialization, failure, and unavailable-entropy behavior.
- [ ] Provide wall-clock time before persistent audit logs require calendar timestamps. Keep monotonic time as the source for elapsed-time and timeout calculations; define behavior when the wall clock is unavailable or invalid.
- [ ] Define kernel/platform shutdown and reboot operations, including filesystem flush ordering and failure behavior. Parse and validate ACPI FADT power-control data when needed; test the supported QEMU shutdown/reboot paths.

**M5a exit criteria:** bounded PCI discovery and the DMA ownership policy are validated for the supported QEMU device path; the block driver passes bounded request, timeout, and error tests; a reproducible image mounts the documented filesystem read-only, with lookup/read tests covering malformed metadata and device errors. No writable mount is implied.

**M5b exit criteria:** writable filesystem behavior is validated across remount and reboot, including crash/failure injection, corruption refusal, I/O errors, and exhausted-space behavior; permission and sticky-directory rules, CSPRNG failure behavior, wall-clock fallback, and supported ACPI shutdown/reboot paths are tested. Milestone 5 validates storage through test/integration harnesses; user-space utilities are verified in Milestone 6.

---

## Milestone 6 — initial userspace and command-line utilities

Crabshell is currently an in-kernel parser/frontend. The long-term terminal application should reuse its parser model without linking kernel internals or bypassing syscalls.

The planned filesystem layout is illustrated below. This is a directory-layout proposal, not a claim that these paths or services are implemented; `/dev`, `/proc`, and `/sys` are intended system interfaces, while `/tmp` and `/run` are volatile.

```text
/
├── boot/
├── dev/
├── etc/
├── home/
│   ├── Public/  (created when a second account is added)
│   └── test/
│       ├── Apps/
│       ├── Desktop/
│       ├── Documents/
│       ├── Downloads/
│       ├── Pictures/
│       ├── Videos/
│       ├── .bin/
│       ├── .config/
│       └── .local/
├── media/
├── mnt/
├── proc/
├── root/
├── run/
├── sys/
├── tmp/
├── usr/
│   ├── Apps/
│   ├── bin/
│   └── sbin/
└── var/
    └── log/
```

### Planned work

- [ ] Build on the minimal `init` process and syscall/runtime foundations from Milestone 4. Establish executable search, environment, current directory, descriptor inheritance, and process startup rules using the VFS.
- [ ] Design a local-account and privilege model. Reserve UID/GID 0 for root, IDs 1–999 for future system/service accounts, and assign regular users IDs starting at 1000; initially give each user a primary group with the same ID. Use local username/password authentication, with a reviewed password-hashing implementation, a unique salt, and the Milestone 5 CSPRNG; Argon2id is a candidate, but exact implementation and parameters require a later security review. Never store plaintext passwords.
- [ ] Create the first regular account through installation or first-boot setup and grant it administrator privileges. Later accounts are standard users by default; root can explicitly grant or revoke administrator status. Run a text login prompt on the serial/terminal console and start the shell under the authenticated user's identity. Do not permit direct root login during normal operation; GUI login is deferred to the GUI milestone.
- [ ] Create `/home/{username}/` for each regular user and `/root/` for the root account. Give regular-user homes `Apps/`, `Desktop/`, `Documents/`, `Downloads/`, `Pictures/`, `Videos/`, `.local/`, `.config/`, and `.bin/` directories. Homes and newly created files are private by default. Use owner/group/other read, write, and execute permissions initially; defer ACLs.
- [ ] Create `/home/Public/` when a second account is added. All users may read it and add files; only a file's owner or root may change or remove that file. Implement and test this with sticky-directory semantics rather than ordinary `rwx` bits alone.
- [ ] Keep `/etc` and `/usr` root-owned and writable only by root. Normal users may read configuration and execute permitted programs. Store readable account metadata separately from password hashes, which must be in a root-only credential file. Global `.app` files go in `/usr/Apps/`; global `.bin` tools go in `/usr/bin/`.
- [ ] Provide a root-only `userctl` command-line tool for creating, disabling, removing, and administering accounts, changing passwords, and granting or revoking administrator privileges. Account removal disables login but preserves the home directory unless file deletion is explicitly requested.
- [ ] Provide designated, administrator-controlled recovery media that can reset any local account, including an administrator account, without a separate recovery secret in the initial design. Document that this alone does not protect against physical attackers; secure boot and disk encryption are separate future security work.
- [ ] Restrict `sudo` to administrators; require the invoking administrator's password for every invocation, with no credential caching. Run the requested command as root using a restricted trusted command path, not the caller's environment. Add increasing delays after repeated failed password attempts rather than permanent account lockout. Record successful and failed privileged actions in `/var/log/` without logging passwords.
- [ ] Establish normal command lookup order as `~/.bin/` before `/usr/bin/`; `sudo` must use its restricted trusted system path instead of inheriting the user's search path.
- [ ] Port or adapt Crabshell into a userspace terminal application that uses only the documented syscall/VFS interfaces. Introduce TTY and PTY abstractions for serial and later graphical terminals so the shell does not depend on a specific device.
- [ ] Move `cp`, `mv`, `mkdir`, and future command-line utilities into separate application crates using the shared userspace runtime and `.bin` suffix. Preinstall the initial tools in the reproducible system image. Later per-user installation copies files into `~/.bin/`; global installation into `/usr/bin/` requires root. Never silently overwrite a same-named tool; defer package management, dependency tracking, and automatic updates.
- [ ] Track the installed image size and per-binary contributions as the static utility set grows. Keep `librustix` lean and `no_std`-friendly, avoid duplicating embedded resources across tools, and set explicit image/storage budgets before adding many separately linked utilities.
- [ ] Add bounded pipe buffers and a minimal process-control model: foreground process groups, `SIGINT` for `Ctrl+C`, `SIGCHLD`/wait status for child exit, and a basic `kill` mechanism. Implement these before enabling pipelines, redirection, or interrupting a foreground command. Keep semantics explicit and tested rather than claiming full POSIX job control.
- [ ] Add command-line quoting, escaping, and history only with parser tests; enable redirection and pipelines only after the corresponding descriptor, pipe, TTY/PTY, and signal semantics are implemented.
- [ ] Defer installation of single-file GUI `.app` files into `~/Apps/` or `/usr/Apps/` to the GUI milestone. Initial installation there is copying a file and removal is deleting it; global installation requires root, and name conflicts must never silently overwrite an existing app.
- [ ] Add administrator-only `shutdown` and `reboot` user commands as separate `.bin` command crates, using the Milestone 5 kernel/platform operations.
- [ ] Add integration tests for login identity, account-ID allocation, password verification and failure delays, private homes, `/home/Public/` sticky-directory behavior, `/etc` and `/usr` write restrictions, `sudo` authorization and trusted command lookup, `userctl` authorization, account recovery, process signals/wait status, pipes, foreground `Ctrl+C`, and launching tools as user processes. Verify password hashes are not exposed and credentials never appear in logs.

**Exit criteria:** the userspace shell and basic `.bin` tools run as isolated processes from a reproducible filesystem image using the shared userspace runtime; local login and account administration enforce the documented identity and permission model; account, `sudo`, recovery, TTY, process-control, and command-launch tests pass; no shell command directly calls kernel-private VFS internals.

## Milestone 7 — ARM64 (AArch64) platform support (long-term)

The current implementation targets x86_64. Add ARM64 as a separate platform backend without weakening the existing x86_64 path or implying feature parity. Start with one documented emulator configuration and expand only when its boot, memory, interrupt, and device contracts are validated.

### Planned work

- [ ] Select and document the initial AArch64 execution environment, firmware/boot protocol, Rust target, linker layout, entry state, and supported CPU/platform assumptions. Use QEMU `virt` as the first repeatable emulator target.
- [ ] Add an isolated AArch64 architecture backend and target-specific build/boot configuration; preserve the working x86_64 target and share code only where the architecture-independent contract is clear.
- [ ] Establish a minimal boot path with bounded serial diagnostics and validated boot metadata, kernel-image bounds, stack state, and usable-memory ownership. Reject unsupported or malformed handoff state visibly.
- [ ] Implement the architecture-specific exception/vector setup, translation-table and cache-maintenance operations, timer, and interrupt-controller path required by the kernel's supported runtime. Keep privileged instructions and raw MMIO access narrow and documented.
- [ ] Adapt the existing kernel services incrementally to explicit architecture interfaces. Keep features unavailable on AArch64 disabled rather than silently approximating their behavior.
- [ ] Add host tests for architecture-independent policy and repeatable AArch64 QEMU tests for boot, diagnostics, memory setup, and configured interrupt/timer behavior. Track physical-hardware validation separately.

**Exit criteria:** the documented AArch64 QEMU target boots the Rustix kernel through a validated platform initialization path, runs the explicitly supported kernel services with integration evidence, and leaves the existing x86_64 validation path passing. This milestone does not claim userspace or full feature parity across architectures.

---

## Milestone 8 — graphical console and GUI (long-term)

A GUI is intentionally downstream of stable memory management, interrupts/input, process isolation, drivers, and userspace. Keep Crabshell's parser independent so a graphical terminal frontend can reuse it.

### Planned work

- [ ] Add validated framebuffer discovery and memory ownership; implement a minimal text/graphics console without compromising serial panic diagnostics.
- [ ] Establish an input subsystem that separates raw device events from key mapping and terminal policy. Plan PS/2 and USB HID support separately; do not treat the current raw scancode poller as a keyboard driver stack.
- [ ] Define a graphics buffer ownership/presentation API, clipping rules, pixel format, and bounds/overflow checks.
- [ ] Implement a minimal compositor/windowing policy only after process isolation and input routing are ready.
- [ ] Define and launch single-file `.app` GUI applications using the documented static ELF64 format and shared userspace runtime; specify how any required resources are embedded.
- [ ] Support drag-and-drop installation of a `.app` file into `~/Apps/`; global installation into `/usr/Apps/` requires root. Reject malformed apps and never silently overwrite an existing file.
- [ ] Run Crabshell as a terminal application in a GUI window using the same parser and userspace services as the serial/TTY path, backed by the TTY/PTY interface rather than direct device access.
- [ ] Preserve serial as a headless recovery/debug console and add repeatable QEMU display/input tests.

**Exit criteria:** a documented GUI session starts from userspace, renders a terminal, accepts tested input, and does not require direct kernel-private VFS access.

---

## Milestone 9 — networking (long-term, after drivers and process isolation)

Networking is not implied by the current device drivers. The initial target should be a tightly scoped virtual-device path with clear ownership and bounded buffers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Build on the PCI discovery and DMA ownership/mapping foundations established in Milestone 5; add only networking-specific device and buffer policy here.
- [ ] Implement one virtual NIC driver with bounded queues and timeouts; test against QEMU user networking.
- [ ] Choose and document a minimal link/network protocol scope before implementation. Keep packet parsing length-checked and fuzzable on the host.
- [ ] Add interface configuration, routing, socket/descriptor ownership, and per-process access policy.
- [ ] Add adversarial packet tests and integration tests for link loss, malformed packets, queue exhaustion, and device reset.
- [ ] Add higher-level transports/services only when the required protocol semantics, tested CSPRNG/entropy-source behavior, and security model are designed.

**Exit criteria:** documented user processes can communicate through a tested virtual NIC/network stack, with malformed input and resource exhaustion handled safely. Do not claim internet, TLS, or POSIX sockets merely from a packet driver.

---

## Milestone 10 — installation, updates, and physical security (long-term)

This milestone depends on persistent storage. Local installation and update workflows can precede networking; remote update-server integration additionally depends on the networking and GUI milestones. Recovery media by itself is not protection against physical attackers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Define a reproducible installer for placing Rustix on a target disk, including partition/boot setup, first-boot account creation, failure handling, and recovery. Preserve a supported local/offline install path.
- [ ] Define system upgrade transactions with integrity checks, safe interruption behavior, and rollback or recovery after a failed upgrade. Do not report success until changes are durable.
- [ ] Add a package manager for both `.app` GUI applications and `.bin` command-line tools. Support per-user and system-wide installation/removal; system-wide changes require root. Keep package/dependency metadata and file ownership consistent with the filesystem policy.
- [ ] Require signed update metadata and packages, verified before installation. Trust Rustix's official signing keys for system updates; require explicit user trust for third-party user-app publishers or repositories. In-app updaters must use the same verification policy.
- [ ] Route system-application updates through Rustix system updates and the package manager. Allow user-installed applications to update through either a verified in-app updater or the package manager.
- [ ] Once networking and the GUI are available, let the GUI check an update server and fetch eligible system and application updates. Keep the local/offline update path available.
- [ ] Design secure boot, disk encryption, and key recovery as long-term physical-security goals. Specify the threat model and recovery-key policy before claiming protection against physical attackers.

**Exit criteria:** a documented local installation and upgrade path recovers safely from interrupted or invalid updates; package signatures and repository trust are enforced; and physical-security claims match the implemented boot and key-protection mechanisms.

---

## Cross-cutting acceptance gates

Every milestone should include the relevant subset of these gates:

1. **Design:** documented ownership, invariants, resource limits, error semantics, and unsupported cases.
2. **Tests:** host tests for pure policy and malformed/boundary input; integration tests for hardware-facing behavior.
3. **Safety:** review unsafe blocks, pointer provenance/access, integer overflow, privilege boundaries, concurrency, and cleanup/rollback paths.
4. **Build:** format, host tests, target check, and final ELF link as appropriate.
5. **Boot/integration:** QEMU tests for changes to boot, paging, descriptors, interrupts, drivers, processes, or persistence.
6. **Documentation/status:** update architecture and roadmap docs; never check off a criterion without evidence.
7. **Compatibility:** claim Unix/POSIX behavior only for the exact documented subset with conformance-style tests.
8. **Privilege boundaries:** test user/kernel fault separation, file ownership and special permission bits, credential confidentiality, trusted `sudo` command lookup, and recovery assumptions.
9. **Resource readiness:** do not begin process, VFS-cache, or driver workloads that require dynamic allocation, active mappings, DMA, wall-clock time, or secure randomness until the corresponding service and failure behavior are validated.

## Working rule

Prefer a small end-to-end vertical slice over broad, unbootable scaffolding. A source file, interface, or architecture document is not proof that the corresponding subsystem is operational. When a check cannot run, record the exact environment blocker and leave that acceptance gate pending.

   165	- [ ] Add timer-driven preemption only after locking, stack, timer, wait-queue, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests. Verify that a non-yielding task is preempted and that IRQ/exception paths cannot deadlock on locks held by interrupted code. This is a hard prerequisite for running general Ring 3 programs in Milestone 4. SMP remains a separate later sub-milestone.
   166	- [x] Implement interrupt-driven UART RX and PS/2 raw-scancode queues with bounded buffers and scheduler event wakeups; preserve polling fallback. OVMF `input-smoke` sends a shell command over UART and verifies a PS/2 make scancode after the shell blocks for input.
   167	
   168	**Exit criteria:** the single-vCPU QEMU `q35` configuration validates the selected APIC routing, PIT tick, and IRQ acknowledgement; host/QEMU tests cover ACPI bounds and malformed tables, mapping rollback/TLB behavior, heap exhaustion, wait-queue wakeups, and cooperative context switching. Interrupt-driven input is tested without busy-polling, and no heap allocation occurs in IRQ/exception context. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

   170	---
   171	
   172	## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI
   173	
   174	Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions. Ring 3 execution is blocked on completing Milestone 3's IRQ-safe locking and timer-preemption items: a non-yielding user task must not be able to monopolize the machine, and preemption must not introduce interrupt-time lock deadlocks.
   175	
   176	### Planned work
   177	
   178	- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path. If using `SYSCALL`/`SYSRET`, specify `SWAPGS` entry/exit state transitions and how exceptions/NMIs during the transition are handled; validate user `RCX` (return RIP) and `RSP` canonicality and bounds before `SYSRET`, and use a safe `IRETQ` path or terminate/reject malformed returns when required.
   179	- [ ] Define per-process address-space construction without deep-cloning the entire kernel page-table tree for every process. Choose a validated kernel-half sharing policy (for example, shared upper-level entries backed by immutable kernel subtrees), while keeping user mappings process-private; specify table ownership/lifetime, teardown, permission invariants, and TLB invalidation before sharing any page-table levels.
   180	- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
   181	- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
   182	- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
   183	- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
   184	- [ ] Load statically linked ELF64 executables with checked `PT_LOAD` bounds, alignment, permissions, and entry points; reject malformed binaries safely. Use `.bin` for command-line programs and `.app` for GUI applications as role-based filename suffixes for the same underlying format. `.app` is a Rustix single-file application suffix, not an Apple/macOS app bundle; initially require application resources to be embedded or absent.
   185	- [ ] Add user-mode exception handling: faults attributable to Ring 3 terminate the offending process with a reported status, while faults in kernel mode remain fatal. Test page faults, general-protection faults, invalid opcodes, and divide errors from both privilege levels.
   186	- [ ] Define user virtual-memory regions, stack bounds/guard behavior, and a minimal anonymous allocation interface such as `mmap`/`munmap` (or a documented equivalent) before running general user programs. Add bounds, permissions, exhaustion, and teardown tests.
   187	- [ ] Add a small, `no_std`-friendly shared userspace runtime crate (for example, `librustix`) for process entry, syscall wrappers, panic handling, common I/O/formatting, and a user allocator backed by the anonymous mapping interface. Keep it separate from kernel internals and use it from independent application crates; initial executables remain statically linked ELF64 binaries, with application resources embedded or absent.
   188	- [ ] Keep the first user-visible target as a minimal `init` executable loaded from a bounded boot payload or other reproducible non-filesystem source; persistent filesystem loading and ordinary command utilities follow in Milestones 5 and 6.
   189	- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, user/kernel fault separation, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.
   190	
   191	### First user-visible target
   192	
   193	A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.
   194	
   195	**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.
   196	
   197	---
   198	
   199	## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership
   200	
   201	Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.
   202	
   203	### M5a — PCI/DMA, block I/O, and read-only/basic VFS
   204	
   205	- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
   206	- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
   207	- [ ] Establish bounded PCI/device discovery, including checked ACPI MCFG handling where required, before adding PCI-backed devices. Keep discovery separate from individual driver policy.
   208	- [ ] Define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, device reset, and error handling before any device can DMA into kernel memory. Scope and test the trust assumptions; do not equate PCI enumeration with safe DMA.
   209	- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk) on top of the shared PCI/DMA foundations.
   210	- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format before implementing writable storage. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior; begin with a read-only mount and bounded metadata parsing.
   211	- [ ] Test read-only mount, lookup, and read behavior against reproducible images, including malformed metadata and I/O errors. Do not expose write operations in this slice.
   212	- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing filesystem operations to applications.
   213	
   214	### M5b — writable filesystem, permissions, and platform services
   215	
   216	- [ ] On detected corruption, report the failure and refuse writable mounting rather than attempting automatic repair. Plan a separate offline checker/repair tool; do not repair data implicitly.
   217	- [ ] Define crash-safe atomic replacement or equivalent transactional behavior for critical files such as account metadata and credentials. Flush the new data before replacing the old file, and test interruption at each update stage.
   218	- [ ] Define explicit no-space errors and partial-write behavior. Never silently discard or overwrite existing user data to recover space.
   219	- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot and failure-injection integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.
   220	
   221	- [ ] Define the planned top-level filesystem layout: `/home`, `/root`, `/etc`, `/usr`, `/dev`, `/proc`, `/sys`, `/tmp`, `/var`, `/run`, `/mnt`, `/media`, and `/boot`, plus `/usr/sbin`. Document that `/proc` and `/sys` are future virtual interfaces, `/dev` exposes device interfaces, `/tmp` and `/run` are volatile, and mount-point and boot-file usage depends on later storage/boot design.
   222	- [ ] Specify filesystem ownership and permission metadata. Support owner/group/other read, write, and execute permissions, default creation modes/umask, and the directory sticky bit. Use sticky-directory semantics for `/tmp` (mode equivalent to `01777`) and later `/home/Public/`, so users can create entries without removing or renaming another user's files.
   223	- [ ] Specify that `/etc` and `/usr` are root-owned and writable only by root, while normal users may read configuration and execute permitted programs. Keep readable account metadata separate from a root-only credential file containing password hashes. Reserve `/usr/Apps` for globally installed `.app` GUI applications and `/usr/bin` for globally installed `.bin` command-line tools; `/usr/sbin` is reserved for system-administration tools if needed.
   224	- [ ] Provide a trustworthy CSPRNG before password hashing or security-sensitive random values. Evaluate validated entropy sources (for example, supported CPU randomness instructions or a virtio RNG device) as inputs; do not treat one hardware source alone as a complete CSPRNG. Test initialization, failure, and unavailable-entropy behavior.
   225	- [ ] Provide wall-clock time before persistent audit logs require calendar timestamps. Keep monotonic time as the source for elapsed-time and timeout calculations; define behavior when the wall clock is unavailable or invalid.
   226	- [ ] Define kernel/platform shutdown and reboot operations, including filesystem flush ordering and failure behavior. Parse and validate ACPI FADT power-control data when needed; test the supported QEMU shutdown/reboot paths.
   227	
   228	**M5a exit criteria:** bounded PCI discovery and the DMA ownership policy are validated for the supported QEMU device path; the block driver passes bounded request, timeout, and error tests; a reproducible image mounts the documented filesystem read-only, with lookup/read tests covering malformed metadata and device errors. No writable mount is implied.
   229	
   230	**M5b exit criteria:** writable filesystem behavior is validated across remount and reboot, including crash/failure injection, corruption refusal, I/O errors, and exhausted-space behavior; permission and sticky-directory rules, CSPRNG failure behavior, wall-clock fallback, and supported ACPI shutdown/reboot paths are tested. Milestone 5 validates storage through test/integration harnesses; user-space utilities are verified in Milestone 6.

   273

Use local username/password authentication, with a reviewed password-hashing implementation, a unique salt, and the Milestone 5 CSPRNG; Argon2id is a candidate, but exact implementation and parameters require a later security review. Never store plaintext passwords.

Later accounts are standard users by default; root can explicitly grant or revoke administrator status. Run a text login prompt on the serial/terminal console and start the shell under the authenticated user's identity. Do not permit direct root login during normal operation; GUI login is deferred to the GUI milestone.

Account removal disables login but preserves the home directory unless file deletion is explicitly requested.

Document that this alone does not protect against physical attackers; secure boot and disk encryption are separate future security work.

# Rustix roadmap

This roadmap describes an incremental path from the current bare-metal kernel to a useful Unix-like operating system. It is a dependency plan, not a schedule or a claim of compatibility. Features become current only after the implementation, tests, and exit criteria below agree.

## How to read status

- A checked box means the source/design work exists; it does **not** imply the code compiled, linked, booted, or passed an integration test.
- A milestone is not complete until its stated exit criteria are met and the evidence is recorded.
- Hardware work needs target build and emulator evidence. Host tests cannot validate privileged instructions, bootloader pointers, page tables, device I/O, or exception-entry assembly.
- Future work is intentionally not represented by placeholder APIs or dummy implementations.

## Current status

- **Milestone 0: local exit criteria met from a clean detached worktree; hosted CI observed.** On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 from both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory. On 2026-11-06, GitHub Actions run [#5](https://github.com/JustEthanCodes/rustix/actions/runs/42288095710) completed successfully on `dev` at `770f9c742dd07a00f6b53274ea05a1eca010d146`; its `kernel-and-boot-smoke` job ran `just verify`. This verifies hosted CI on that remote commit, not today’s uncommitted changes.
- **Milestone 1: validation criteria met for the current Limine path.** The bounded boot snapshot, memory-range classification, and CPUID reporting were covered by host tests and QEMU reporting; the Limine pointer-readability trust boundary remains explicit.
- **Milestone 2: local exit criteria met on 2026-10-24; hosted CI observed, physical-hardware validation pending.** The boot path owns and activates a clone of Limine's reachable page-table hierarchy, preserves inherited mappings, hardens kernel HHDM aliases to R/NX or RW/NX while retaining PAT attributes, invalidates stale translations on CR3 transitions, and retains table-frame tokens. `just verify`, `just frame-smoke`, and `just fault-smoke` passed after final review; QEMU exercised the active-PCID/CR3 invalidation path with CR4.PGE clear. The PGE-toggle path is statically reviewed but was not exercised by this QEMU configuration. The successful 2026-11-06 hosted `just verify` run covers the published Milestone 2 state, but not today's uncommitted changes. Broad mapping policy, reclamation, IRQ-safe allocation, and physical-hardware validation remain outside this milestone's completed scope.
- **Milestone 3: local exit criteria met on 2026-11-07; hosted CI and physical-hardware validation remain pending.** `just verify` passed with 127 host tests, the `x86_64-unknown-none` check, BIOS and OVMF boot smokes, active-map/TLB invalidation, cooperative thread/wait-queue tests, and UART/PS/2 input wakeup. OVMF validated MADT/APIC routing, PIT ticks and EOI, guarded cooperative stacks, frame-backed heap growth, and shell input without busy-polling. Timer preemption, IRQ-safe locking for future preemption, and SMP remain deferred. See the evidence and limits below. **Milestones 4 and later: planned.** There is no ARM64 platform support, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, GUI, or networking stack.

## Dependency path

```text
Reliable boot
    -> validated boot state
    -> owned mappings + frame allocation + heap + fault diagnostics
    -> timer/IRQ model + scheduler + IRQ-safe locking + timer preemption
    -> isolated processes + syscall ABI
    -> M5a PCI/DMA + block I/O + read-only/basic VFS
    -> M5b writable filesystem + permissions + platform services
    -> userland utilities
    -> graphical terminal and other optional services
```

Some device-driver work can proceed in parallel after the core ownership, locking, and testing rules exist. It must not bypass them with direct, unreviewed hardware access.

---

## Milestone 0 — repeatable Rust kernel boot (DONE)

### Implementation present

- [x] `no_std` Rust kernel binary for `x86_64-unknown-none` with its own ELF linker layout and `_start`.
- [x] Limine boot requests and documented external-loader boundary.
- [x] COM1 serial output/input, startup reporting, and panic/fatal halt path.
- [x] Narrow x86 port-I/O helpers and raw non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling.
- [x] `just` tasks for formatting, host tests, target checks, ELF/image builds, and QEMU smoke/run workflows.
- [x] Pinned Limine v12.9.3 binary archive with SHA-256 verification, BIOS/UEFI hybrid image recipe, and CI workflow.
- [x] Separate allocation-free Crabshell parser, kernel serial frontend, and bounded volatile RAM filesystem.

### Validation evidence and remaining proof

- [x] Current source passed formatting, host tests, target check, and optimized build through `just verify`.
- [x] The pinned image built and the bounded QEMU smoke test reached the Crabshell prompt in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on 2026-10-16.
- [x] A separate interactive QEMU session exercised `help`, `ls`, `meminfo`, directory navigation, and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations; `cp` replaced an existing destination, `rmdir` refused a nonempty directory, and unsupported `memtest` was rejected as expected.
- [x] Repeat verification from a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory and uncached build/tool state; fresh Limine download/host-tool compilation, image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test all passed on 2026-10-16.
- [x] Observe the hosted CI workflow; GitHub Actions run #5 completed successfully on the published `dev` commit on 2026-11-06 (see run #5 above).

The QEMU serial log showed the startup banner, HHDM offset, validated memory-map summary, frame counts, CPUID report, and initial prompt. The interactive command check is a focused manual test, not exhaustive shell coverage or a persistence test. `cat` returned `hello Rustix from QEMU`, `cp` replaced an existing destination with source data, `rmdir` refused a nonempty directory, and `pwd` returned to `/home/rustix` after cleanup. If a future smoke test fails, preserve `target/rustix-qemu-serial.log` as failure evidence.

**Exit criteria:** met locally. A clean detached worktree with uncached build/tool state built the image, reached `_start`, reported the expected startup state, and reached the Crabshell prompt in the automated QEMU test. Hosted CI was also observed passing on the published commit noted above; it does not imply that later uncommitted changes passed CI.
